/blog/psoriatic-vs-rheumatoid-arthritis.answer: Psoriatic arthritis is linked to psoriasis and can be asymmetric, affecting DIP joints and causing nail changes. If a flare lasts over 7-10 days, or if you develop fever, contact your doctor.

/blog/sleep-quality-arthritis-pain.question: How Sleep Quality Affects Arthritis Pain: What the Research
/blog/sleep-quality-arthritis-pain.answer: Poor sleep can worsen arthritis pain, with up to 80% of rheumatoid arthritis patients experiencing sleep disturbances. This is because inflammatory cytokines peak at night, increasing stiffness, and pain sensitivity increases with sleep deprivation. To improve sleep, maintain consistent bedtimes, keep the bedroom cool (16–18°C), and block blue light before bed. Consider gentle stretching or a warm bath in the evening.

/blog/swimming-for-arthritis.answer: Swimming is beneficial for arthritis as water's buoyancy supports up to 90% of body weight, reducing joint load and pain. Warm water, ideally 28–32°C, relaxes muscles and increases blood flow, while hydrostatic pressure can reduce joint swelling. Regular sessions, starting with 15–20 minutes and building to 30–45 minutes, two to three times weekly, can improve physical function and quality of life.

/blog/turmeric-for-arthritis.question: Turmeric for Arthritis: Does It Really Work?
/blog/turmeric-for-arthritis.answer: Curcumin, turmeric's active compound, has reasonable clinical evidence for arthritis. Around 1,000 mg/day for 8–12 weeks appears to reduce pain and stiffness by blocking the NF-κB and COX-2 inflammatory pathways. Absorption from plain turmeric is poor, so use a piperine, phytosome or liposomal formulation and take with food.

/blog/gut-health-arthritis-connection.answer: The gut microbiome, comprising trillions of bacteria, significantly influences inflammation and immune function crucial for arthritis. An imbalance in gut bacteria, known as dysbiosis, may trigger or worsen autoimmune responses. Increased intestinal permeability ("leaky gut") allows bacterial fragments into the bloodstream, causing widespread inflammation. Dietary changes, such as consuming prebiotic and probiotic foods, can support a diverse and healthy gut microbiome.

It strengthens muscles without joint impact, improves balance, and reduces pain and stress. Benefits typically emerge after 6–8 weeks of regular practice, with sessions often lasting 45–60 minutes. Many classes teach the Tai Chi for Arthritis programme, specifically designed for people with joint conditions.

/blog/travelling-with-arthritis-uk.question: Travelling with Arthritis: A UK Guide to Pain-Free Holidays
/blog/travelling-with-arthritis-uk.answer: To travel with arthritis, consult your GP or rheumatologist at least six weeks before your trip to discuss medication and time zone changes. Always declare arthritis on travel insurance. Pack double the medication, split between hand and hold luggage. During travel, request assistance, stand and stretch frequently, and consider accessible destinations. Planning, pacing, and permission to rest are key for a comfortable journey.

/blog/gout-medication-uk.question: Gout Medication UK: A Complete Guide to Drugs for Gout
/blog/gout-medication-uk.answer: For acute gout attacks, common treatments include NSAIDs like naproxen (500mg twice daily) or indomethacin, which reduce inflammation and pain. Colchicine, taken as 1mg initially then 500 micrograms one hour later, is an alternative, especially if NSAIDs are unsuitable. If these are ineffective, corticosteroids such as prednisolone (30-35mg daily for 3-5 days) can be used.

/blog/managing-arthritis-flare-ups-at-ho.question: Managing Arthritis Flare-Ups at Home
/blog/managing-arthritis-flare-ups-at-ho.answer: Managing arthritis flare-ups involves a multi-pronged approach at home. Regularly take paracetamol (up to 4g daily) or suitable NSAIDs, and use topical treatments. Apply heat for stiffness, cold for swelling. Balance rest for acutely inflamed joints with gentle movement and short walks. Create an action plan: for mild flares, increase pain relief; for moderate, reduce activities; for severe, contact your GP, especially if lasting over 3-5 days.

/blog/ginger-vs-turmeric-for-arthritis.title: Ginger vs Turmeric for Arthritis: Which Actually Works? | Living With Arthritis UK
/blog/ginger-vs-turmeric-for-arthritis.description: Ginger vs turmeric for arthritis: a UK clinician compares the evidence, doses, safety, and which one actually helps joint pain.
/blog/ginger-vs-turmeric-for-arthritis.question: Ginger vs Turmeric for Arthritis: Which Actually Works?
/blog/ginger-vs-turmeric-for-arthritis.answer: For most people with arthritis, turmeric (as a properly absorbed curcumin supplement at around 1,000 mg/day for 8–12 weeks) has the stronger evidence for reducing pain and stiffness. Ginger at 500–1,000 mg/day is a well-tolerated adjunct, especially if you also have morning stiffness or nausea. Check with your GP before starting.

/blog/arthritis-and-pregnancy-uk.question: Arthritis and Pregnancy in the UK
/blog/arthritis-and-pregnancy-uk.answer: Managing arthritis during pregnancy requires careful planning with your rheumatologist. Some medications like methotrexate must be stopped months before conception, while others like hydroxychloroquine are considered safe. Folic acid (400 micrograms daily) should be started at least three months prior. Regular monitoring throughout pregnancy and planning for potential postpartum flares are crucial for a healthy outcome.

/blog/lower-back-stiffness-worse-after-s.description: Prolonged sitting compresses lumbar discs and tightens hip flexors that pull on the spine. Why standing up hurts and what helps within 60 seconds.
/blog/lower-back-stiffness-worse-after-s.question: Lower Back Stiffness: Why It Is Worse After Sitting
/blog/lower-back-stiffness-worse-after-s.answer: Lower back stiffness after sitting can stem from various factors, including the condition of joint cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments, muscles, and nerves. Inflammatory arthritis typically worsens with rest, while degenerative arthritis worsens with prolonged use. Gentle movement and structured exercise, around 150 minutes weekly, often help. Other beneficial approaches include anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat applications, and ensuring adequate sleep.

/blog/working-with-arthritis-uk-rights.question: Working with Arthritis – Your UK Employment Rights
/blog/working-with-arthritis-uk-rights.answer: If your arthritis significantly affects daily activities, it's considered a disability under the Equality Act 2010. This protects you from discrimination and harassment at work. Your employer must make reasonable adjustments, such as flexible hours or ergonomic equipment. The Access to Work scheme can also fund equipment and support. You are entitled to Statutory Sick Pay if you need time off.

/blog/driving-with-arthritis-uk.answer: You must inform the DVLA if your arthritis affects your ability to drive safely, for example, if you have difficulty gripping the steering wheel, operating pedals, or checking mirrors. Not all arthritis requires reporting; only if it impacts driving. Vehicle adaptations like steering wheel aids or automatic transmission can help. If eligible, the Motability Scheme provides adapted cars, and a Blue Badge offers parking concessions.

This link is due to factors like chronic pain, loss of independence, social isolation, and fatigue. Warning signs include persistent low mood or withdrawing from others. /blog/how-to-sleep-with-arthritis-uk.question: How to Sleep Better with Arthritis
/blog/how-to-sleep-with-arthritis-uk.answer: To sleep better with arthritis, adjust your sleep position, use a medium-firm mattress, and consider a supportive pillow. For knee arthritis, place a pillow between or under your knees. For hip arthritis, sleep on your non-affected side with a pillow between knees. Timing pain medication to be effective at night, maintaining good sleep hygiene, and relaxing before bed can also help.

/blog/arthritis-and-diet-myths-uk.answer: There is no strong evidence that nightshade vegetables or dairy products generally worsen arthritis. While turmeric has anti-inflammatory properties, it is not a cure. Excess sugar, however, drives inflammation and weight gain, which can worsen arthritis. Red meat should be reduced, but lean red meat in moderation provides essential nutrients. The best approach is a balanced, Mediterranean-style diet.

/blog/hydrotherapy-pools-uk.answer: Hydrotherapy is exercising in warm water, typically between 33-36°C, to relieve arthritis symptoms. The warmth relaxes muscles and eases pain, while water's buoyancy supports body weight, reducing joint stress. Benefits include pain relief, reduced stiffness, muscle strengthening, and improved balance. Access hydrotherapy through NHS physiotherapy referrals or community leisure centres offering warm water sessions.

Effective management takes a whole-person approach: exercise, sensible medication use, heat and cold therapy, and mindfulness. Prioritising sleep, setting realistic daily goals, and having a plan for flare-ups reduces pain and improves well-being. If pain affects your mood, speak to your GP.

It strengthens supporting muscles like quadriceps, glutes, and hamstrings, while improving joint range of motion through gentle, repetitive pedalling. It is different from normal ageing, as many older people remain robust. Clinically, frailty is identified by unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking speed, and low physical activity. Early identification is crucial for effective intervention and improved outcomes.

/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-.answer: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function, and enhancing quality of life. This integrated approach, which combines medication with movement, is recommended in clinical guidelines. Exercise is thought to lower widespread inflammation, maintain healthy weight, strengthen muscles, and improve mood, all of which support treatment response.

/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthrit.question: Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010
/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthrit.answer: Arthritis can impact work performance due to its effects on physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. Many individuals with arthritis work successfully, often with workplace adjustments. Reasonable adjustments, which are a legal entitlement, include flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, and adjusted duties. You do not have to disclose your arthritis to your employer unless it poses a health and safety risk.

/blog/juvenile-arthritis-uk.question: Juvenile Arthritis UK: A Parent's Guide to Childhood Joint C
/blog/juvenile-arthritis-uk.answer: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a group of autoimmune conditions causing joint inflammation in children under 16, affecting approximately 15,000 children and young people in the UK. Parents might notice limping, morning stiffness, swollen joints, or unusual irritability. Diagnosis involves clinical assessment by a paediatric rheumatologist. Treatment aims for remission, using medicines like NSAIDs, methotrexate, and biologics, alongside physiotherapy to maintain joint function and strength.

/blog/foot-and-ankle-arthritis-uk.answer: Foot and ankle arthritis symptoms vary by type but commonly include pain, stiffness, and swelling. For big toe arthritis, you might notice difficulty walking and a bony bump. Ankle arthritis often causes deep pain, stiffness in the morning, and swelling. Rheumatoid arthritis in the feet can lead to pain under the ball of the foot and toe deformities, affecting up to 90% of those with RA.
